paper_title: PhysEvo: Astra Can Act, Let It

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Astra can act, yet reliable manipulation depends on the system through which it observes and controls the world. We introduce PhysEvo, a framework for physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) around a single frozen model. A task agent executes robot tasks; a meta-agent uses the resulting trajectories to diagnose failures, revise tools and skills, and test corrections. The meta-agent can also improve its own diagnostic tools, so retained revisions support both later action and later self-improvement. This process develops joint-level control, evidence-seeking observation, and reusable manipulation skills without model-weight updates or a separately trained action policy. Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, held-out-layout evaluation of retained task-specific deployment versions yields a five-dimension average score of 68.14/100 and 62.00% success, compared with 47.17% for RoboDawn's one-shot Astra agent, the strongest published reference in our comparison. On eight manipulation tasks challenging direct Astra, PhysEvo achieves 55.00% success, compared with 1.25% for the direct-Astra reference. Deploying the simulation-evolved harness on AgileX PiPER and continuing skill revision yields 90.60/100 average score and 84.00% success across 25 trials on five real-world tasks. PhysEvo turns the consequences of action into persistent, testable changes to how a frozen model acts and improves.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Astra can already control robot, but demonstrated competence does not guarantee reliable execution. In ten-task RoboDojo evaluation, direct Astra reaches 100% success on object classification yet succeeds on only 26% of attempts overall. Pairing it with the specialized visionlanguageaction (VLA) policy π0.5 raises success to 48% (Su et al., 2026). These results pose question: what prevents capabilities that are already present from being used reliably? Our executions expose bottlenecks in the harness: the tools, skills, and execution logic between the model and the robot. During pouring, the held bottle obscures the wrist view needed to monitor liquid delivery. With tool-center-point (TCP) interface, local inverse kinematics (IK) can fold the arm into an obstructive posture, while leaving Astra no explicit way to choose the joint configuration (figures 3 and 4). These failures call for more than new action through an unchanged interface: the agent needs useful view or direct authority over posture. Why should the same model be able to fix failure it did not prevent? Retrospective diagnosis has access to evidence that was unavailable during action selection. trajectory reveals the consequences of command; aligned images, robot states, and code help trace those consequences to cause. Astra can then propose concrete intervention, such as maintaining free-arm side view or exposing joint reconfiguration, and test it through further execution. In our pouring case, revised skill guidance changes the observation strategy, and the subsequent episode succeeds. Physical interaction thus provides both evidence for correction and test of whether it works. correction need not end with the episode. Retained tools and skills change later execution; retained diagnostic tools change how later failures can be investigated. In our packing case, Astra reuses review tool it built earlier to trace box displacement to preceding contact and revise clearance guidance (figure 5). We call this loop physical recursive self-improvement (RSI): experience revises the system used for action and diagnosis, and the revised system is inherited by subsequent rounds. We introduce PhysEvo, which implements this loop with one frozen Astra in two roles. The task agent observes and controls the robot. The meta-agent inspects execution, edits tools and skills, tests revisions, and retains useful changes, including changes to its own diagnostic resources. The resulting framework combines joint-level control, active and historical observation, geometry tools, and manipulation skills. Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, held-out-layout evaluation of retained task-specific deployment versions achieves 68.14/100 score and 62.00% success under equal five-dimension weighting. This exceeds the 47.17% reported by RoboDawns one-shot Astra agent, the strongest reference in our comparison  (table 1)  (Guo et al., 2026a). On the ten-task comparison with direct and hybrid policies, PhysEvo reaches 68.00% success versus 26.00% and 48.00%, respectively. On eight manipulation tasks challenging direct Astra, it reaches 55.00% versus 1.25%, 53.75-point gain; Simate-beta, the strongest robot-policy reference on this subset, reports 50.83% (figure 1 and table 3) (RoboDojo Team, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026d). On AgileX PiPER, the simulation-evolved harness serves as starting point for continued adaptation. Across five trials on each of five real-world tasks, PhysEvo achieves mean score of 90.60/100 and 84.00% success. Revisions compensate for liquid-flow effects and replace geometry-first localization with visually guided approach followed by close-range geometric refinement (section 5.6). The same loop can therefore revise both how the robot moves and when it seeks geometric evidence. 2 Our contributions are (i) physical RSI framework in which one frozen model acts, revises, and inherits task and meta resources; (ii) an evolved interaction architecture combining joint control, evidence-seeking observation, and reusable skills; and (iii) 42-task evaluation with mechanism-focused cases and five-task evaluation of continued adaptation on real hardware.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Foundation models for robot control. Visionlanguageaction models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and π0.5 learn control from robot data (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Code as Policies instead composes perception and control APIs, while Inner Monologue incorporates environmental feedback (Liang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2022). CaP-X and Guava study tool, action, and observation design (Fu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a); Show-Harness and obstacle-aware harnesses address embodiment and geometric constraints (Chen et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). RoboDawn couples discrete commands with feedback and demonstrations (Guo et al., 2026a). Thea and PhyAgentOS structure persistent state and outcome verification (Wang et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026b), while Harness VLA and RoboHarness use execution memory to guide primitives or route heterogeneous policies (Zhang et al., 2026e; Huang et al., 2026). These systems establish the importance of the interface around model. Self-improving agents. Reflexion retains verbal feedback, and GEPA evolves prompts from execution traces (Shinn et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2025). ADAS searches code-defined agents; SICA and DGM modify agent implementations (Hu et al., 2024; Robeyns et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). AutoHarness, Meta-Harness, and Self-Harness synthesize or revise executable harnesses from feedback (Lou et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a). Recursive Harness Self-Improvement evolves prompt-level harness with fixed optimizer (Lee et al., 2026a), whereas STOP and Hyperagents also modify the improvement procedure (Zelikman et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026b). RRSI regularizes harness edits, and Dream-RSI uses discovery histories to improve exploration (Xia et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026). Hyperagents robotics experiment evolves rewards for PPO controllers (Zhang et al., 2026b, App. C.3); PhysEvo instead uses the same frozen model for robot decisions and software revision. Experience-driven embodied agents. REFLECT diagnoses failures from execution summaries (Liu et al., 2023); Voyager and RATs accumulate executable skills through interaction and autonomous play (Wang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026c). EmbodiSkill distinguishes faulty skills from failures to follow valid guidance (Ju et al., 2026); ASPIRE retains manipulation and debugging knowledge from multimodal traces (Lu et al., 2026). RoboRSI organizes skills hierarchically (Noematrix Team, 2026), and Zetta evolves critics, recovery, and tools around frozen action policy (Ding et al., 2026). SHAPER evolves skills and context-construction code with one frozen model serving as planner and optimizer, while fixing the action interface and executor (Wang et al., 2026a). ENPIRE automates real-world policy development (Xiao et al., 2026). RHO evolves multi-file robot repositories, including prompts, tools, and control code for LLM-in-the-loop execution (Elmaaroufi et al., 2026). HarnessPAI revises programs and repair skills across rollouts, keeping the selected high-level program fixed within each rollout (Wang et al., 2026c). PhysEvo focuses on the joint evolution of skills, robot-facing action and observation interfaces, and diagnostic resources: the same frozen model acts through revised interfaces and reuses self-built tools to diagnose later failures.

sections.title: 3 PHYSEVO: PHYSICAL RECURSIVE SELF-IMPROVEMENT
sections.content: PhysEvo alternates between acting in the environment and revising the system used to act. single frozen model performs both roles. Physical outcomes provide evidence; tested changes to the harness preserve what is learned from that evidence (figure 2). Figure 2: Physical RSI in PhysEvo. frozen Astra acts through the task harness and revises both task and meta resources from execution feedback. Accepted revisions support later episodes and improvement rounds.

sections.title: 3.1 ONE FROZEN MODEL, TWO EDITABLE HARNESSES
sections.content: Let Mθ denote Astra with fixed parameters. At iteration r, the persistent system consists of task harness task and meta harness meta : Hr = (H task , meta ). (1) The task harness supplies observations, action tools, execution feedback, and skills. Task-agnostic skills guide operations such as grasp verification and recovery; task-specific skills guide activities such as pouring or packing. The meta harness provides code inspection and editing, trajectory review, diagnostic experiments, and revision testing. The meta-agent may modify either harness, including its own tools. The two roles use separate contexts and tool access but the same model. Model weights, robot dynamics, and the task evaluator are not editable. Initialization provides working observationaction loop with TCP targets and local IK, plus general codeediting workspace. From this starting point, the system develops joint-level control, specialized observation tools, and reusable skills through execution and revision.

sections.title: 3.2 TASK EXECUTION AND PHYSICAL FEEDBACK
sections.content: The task agent receives the instruction, selected skills, camera images, and robot proprioception. It selects an action or observation tool, then uses the returned result to make its next decision. Observation tools can retrieve evidence or calculate geometry without advancing the environment. Motion tools execute commands and return the resulting state and images. 4 For diagnosis, the harness links each requested action to its dispatched command and observed outcome. An unsuccessful grasp can thus be examined through approach, gripper closure, and subsequent object motion, rather than reduced to final score. During execution, the same feedback supports closed-loop correction within the episode.

sections.title: 3.3 REVISION, TESTING, AND RECURSIVE REUSE
sections.content: The meta-agent reviews execution alongside the current implementation, forms failure hypothesis, and tests it through further inspection or diagnostic experiments. revision may change action or observation tools, execution logic, skills, or diagnostic utilities. When tool changes, its skill guidance is revised with it so that the agent inherits both capability and instructions for using it. Candidate revisions are tested during development, not on the held-out layouts used for final scoring. The meta-agent first checks that edited code runs and tools return the intended outputs. For behavioral changes, it compares the candidate with the current harness on the same task and initial scene. score gain, or progress beyond the failure without score decrease, supports adoption; score decrease leads to rejection. diagnostic-tool revision is checked against the error or measurement it is intended to address. Accepted changes take effect between episodes. Changes to the task harness shape later execution; changes to the meta harness shape later diagnosis and revision. review tool built in one round can therefore support different correction in later round. The improvement process thus inherits changes to its own machinery. retained deployment version is then fixed for that tasks held-out evaluation (section 5.1). Section gives the full procedure.

sections.title: 4 THE EVOLVED EMBODIED FRAMEWORK
sections.content: Physical RSI reshapes what Astra can control, what evidence it can obtain, and what guidance persists. We describe the resulting architecture below; tasks retain their own deployment versions (section 5.1). 4.1 JOINT-LEVEL CONTROL The default control_arms interface accepts twelve absolute arm-joint targets and two continuous gripper commands. It supports both arms and remains available while an object is held. The executor enforces native actuator limits and checks measured motion; Astra chooses the approach, arm configuration, and reconfiguration. TCP control asks the model for an end-effector goal and delegates posture selection to IK. Joint control instead makes posture part of the policy decision. This additional authority lets Astra adjust an obstructive configuration and continue manipulation, rather than repeatedly requesting target from an unsuitable posture. Section C.1 compares the interfaces under fixed model, skill, initialization, and budget.

sections.title: 4.2 ACTIVE AND RETROSPECTIVE OBSERVATION
sections.content: Astra can move free arm to obtain useful wrist-camera view while the other arm manipulates an object. When the relevant event is no longer visible, review_frames retrieves earlier images and aligned robot states from the current episode without advancing physics. Active viewing seeks new evidence; historical retrieval recovers evidence already observed. 5 Pixel projection and multi-view triangulation compute geometry for image features selected by Astra. Temporal triangulation uses views collected as wrist camera moves. The model decides what to inspect and where to look; deterministic tools compute geometry and check validity using images and known camera and robot geometry, not hidden object coordinates. Temporal reconstruction requires stationary point and translational viewing baseline.

sections.title: 4.3 REUSABLE SKILLS AND DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS
sections.content: Skills link tools to the physical conditions under which they are useful: when to verify grasp, obtain another view, reorient an object, clear an obstacle, or check release. The pouring skill, for example, maintains free-arm side view through pouring and upright recovery. packing skill requires wrist and gripper clearance above raised box flaps before turning. Skills retain these lessons while leaving action decisions to Astras closed-loop policy. The meta harness retains trajectory-review tools that align images, robot states, and policy decisions. The task agent uses runtime tools and selected skills; the meta-agent uses the broader editing and diagnostic workspace. Experience is therefore retained in two forms: guidance for acting and tools for understanding why an action failed.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We first evaluate retained deployment versions on held-out simulation layouts, then examine the revisions behind the resulting framework. On real hardware, we continue skill adaptation after deployment.

sections.title: 5.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Tasks and metrics. We evaluate all 42 base RoboDojo simulation tasks across generalization, precision, long-horizon execution, memory, and open-ended instruction following. Native score ranges from 0 to 100; success rate (SR) counts scores of 100. Each task averages one attempt on each of five held-out layouts. The headline comparison weights the five dimensions equally after averaging tasks within each dimension. We also report the equal-task average and two task-level comparisons covering 16 distinct tasks (tables 2 and 3). Development, sharing, and scoring. Simulation self-improvement precedes scoring. Development resources are shared across tasks; at the task-agent level, only tools and task-agnostic skills are shared, while task-specific skills remain task-local. Each task retains deployment version that stays fixed across its five scored layouts. Scored layouts are excluded from revision and version selection. Before each scored episode, we reset session context, historical-frame indices, and writable memory. Online correction and same-episode history are allowed, but persistent tools and skills do not change. Section details these boundaries. Comparison methods. References include RoboDojo robot and language-model policies (RoboDojo Team, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026d), GPT-as-Policys direct Astra and Astraπ0.5 hybrid (Su et al., 2026), and RoboDawns one-shot Astra agent with closed-loop feedback and in-context demonstrations (Guo et al., 2026a). Bold and underlining indicate the best and second-best values within each comparison panel.

This is the highest reported average among the compared methods, including an Astra agent already equipped with feedback and demonstrations. Equal weighting of all 42 tasks instead gives 65.00 score and 58.57% SR. sections.title: 5.5 WHAT CHANGES THROUGH PHYSICAL RSI?
sections.content: Three cases trace execution feedback to concrete changes in control, observation, and diagnosis. Making posture policy decision. Figure 3 shows two independent executions: an obstructive fold under TCP control with local IK, and recovery from rejected TCP motion through joint reconfiguration. End-effector goals leave posture to IK; joint control makes that missing choice expressible. In focused two-layout comparison with the model, skill, initialization, and budget fixed, mean scores are 40 for TCP, 100 for Joint, and 55 for Both (six episodes; section C.1). Joint outperforming Both in this comparison also shows that larger tool menu alone is not sufficient. Figure 3: Joint reconfiguration enables recovery from an obstructive arm posture. Maintaining evidence during action. pouring failure occurs while the bottle blocks the holding arms wrist view. Revising the pouring skill, with the other loaded skills fixed, directs the free arm to maintain side view through pouring and recovery. The task agent then checks the bottle mouth, cup rim, liquid landing point, and clearance, corrects its motion, and completes the task (figure 4). The revised skill keeps existing sensors useful as manipulation alters visibility. 9 Figure 4: Skill revision maintains useful view throughout pouring and recovery. Inheriting means of diagnosis. In figure 5, the meta-agent invokes review tool built in an earlier round. Aligned images, robot states, and policy decisions help trace box displacement to wrist or gripper contact with raised flaps. The skill is then revised to require clearance above the flaps before turning. In the revised execution, the task agent follows this guidance and avoids pushing the box away. The final symptom, box out of reach, thus leads to specific intervention on the preceding contact. Crucially, diagnostic resource created by one improvement round helps produce correction in another: the system inherits way to improve, not only way to act. Figure 5: An inherited review tool supports later packing-skill revision.

sections.title: 5.6 REAL-WORLD ADAPTATION THROUGH SKILL REVISION
sections.content: We deploy the simulation-evolved harness on an AgileX PiPER platform and continue the executionrevision loop. After each attempt, the meta-agent analyzes the trajectory and revises skills; the task agent uses those revisions in the next attempt. These cycles yield successful executions of block stacking, bowl stacking, pen placement, liquid pouring, and writing PhysEvo with pen (figure 6). Hardware results. We report five trials per task, for 25 trials in total  (table 4)  . PhysEvo achieves mean score of 90.60/100 and 84.00% SR. Block stacking, bowl stacking, and pen placement each achieve 100% SR; pouring and writing each achieve 60% SR. Section B.3 specifies the task-level scoring rules. 10 Table 4: Real-world performance on AgileX PiPER. Each task has five trials.

sections.content: 100.00 100.00 100.00 60.00 93.00 90.60 100.00 100.00 100.00 60.00 60.00 84.00 Two revisions illustrate how physical discrepancies change the inherited skills. Compensating for liquid motion. The liquid streams forward momentum causes it to overshoot the cup. The meta-agent revises the pouring skill to shift the bottle opening backward relative to the cup, compensating for the observed displacement. The hardware revision changes the action to account for the observed flow. Changing when geometry is used. Our physical arm has lower positioning accuracy than its simulated counterpart, and localization from the initial distant view is often unreliable. The revised skill reverses the geometry-first sequence: visual feedback guides coarse approach, then geometry provides close-range localization for fine positioning. By changing the order of perception and action, the revised skill uses geometry under more reliable viewing conditions. These cases demonstrate continued post-deployment adaptation. Additional simulation executions appear in section E.

sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
sections.content: PhysEvo uses physical consequences to revise the tools, skills, and diagnostic resources of frozen Astra. Its retained deployment versions achieve 62.00% success under five-dimension weighting across 42 RoboDojo tasks. The cases identify three ways experience changes the system: exposing posture control, maintaining useful observations, and inheriting tools for later diagnosis. On AgileX PiPER, the same loop adapts skills to liquid motion and localization discrepancies, with mean score of 90.60/100 and 84.00% success across five tasks. The central lesson is that experience can improve not only the next action, but the interface and diagnostic resources available to future actions. 11 Figure 6: Five AgileX PiPER tasks after trajectory-driven skill revision. Each row shows one execution in time; alternate final views are marked.

The initial meta harness supplies code-editing and execution workspace. Retained tools and skills form compatible system: an updated tool and the guidance for using its API are loaded together. The task agent uses its runtime tools; the meta-agent uses the code-editing workspace. Development resources are shared across tasks. Their union contains 16 distinct tasks and 80 attempts, giving 75.06 score and 65.00% SR. Each task is counted once in this union; the two subset averages are not averaged together. Development and held-out scoring. Self-improvement takes place during simulation development. For each task, retained deployment version is fixed across its five scored layouts; these layouts are not used for harness revision or version selection. Development resources may carry experience across tasks, but task-agent sharing is restricted to tools and task-agnostic skills. Task-specific skills remain task-local. Episode state and information access. Before every scored episode, session context, historical-frame indices, and writable memory are reset. The task agent loads its retained tools and selected skills, then may accumulate and revisit observations from that episode and correct its actions online. This within-episode feedback does not change persistent tools, skills, or the deployment version. Scored instances do not supply privileged information to the meta-agent or contribute to revision or version selection. The hardware experiments use separate adaptation protocol with skill revision after deployment; section 5.6 reports the real-world trial outcomes. B.2 COMPARISON SOURCES AND AGGREGATION Five-dimension comparison. The robot and direct-language-model results in table 1 are taken from the RoboDojo leaderboard and Astra report (RoboDojo Team, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026d). The final average weights the five dimensions equally. RoboDawns five-dimension Score and SR are computed from its public evaluation records: GPT-6 Astra, 1-shot, with five runs per task (Guo et al., 2026b). The dimension-weighted means, 54.63 score and 47.17% SR, agree with its paper (Guo et al., 2026a). Direct and hybrid Astra policies. The ten-task set follows GPT-as-Policy (Su et al., 2026). PhysEvo is evaluated on five layouts per task, with one attempt per layout, for 50 attempts in total. The source reports 50 selected cases for the hybrid and 48 valid scores for Direct. We recompute Directs score by averaging task means, giving 38.50 rather than its pooled-case score of 37.81. The three VLA methods displayed in table 2 have the highest ten-task average scores among the source reports VLA references. Manipulation-challenge subset. The eight tasks in table 3 correspond to Table F2 of the RoboDojo Astra report (Zhang et al., 2026d). Its selection criterion is VLA SR 20% and Astra SR < 5%. Both Score and SR are shown in the task rows. Section retains the other robot-policy references. 17 B.3 REAL-WORLD SCORES AND SUCCESS CRITERIA Each hardware task is evaluated over five trials. As in simulation, Score summarizes partial and full task completion on 0100 scale, while SR is the percentage of trials reaching the tasks maximum score. Averaging the five task-level metrics in table 4 gives Score of 90.60/100 and an SR of 84.00%. The task-specific scores are defined below. Stack blocks. The goal is to stack three blocks. score of 0 means that no block stacking is completed; 15 means that any two of the three blocks are stacked; 100 requires all three blocks to be stacked and the arm to return home. Stack bowls. The goal is to stack three bowls. score of 0 means that no bowls are correctly stacked; 15 means that any two bowls are stacked upright; 100 requires all three bowls to be stacked upright, the bottom bowl to rest stably on the table, and the arm to return home. Place pens. The goal is to place both pens in the holder. Scores are 0 if neither pen is in the holder, 50 if either one is in the holder, and 100 if both are in the holder. Pour water. The goal is to pour liquid from the bottle into the cup. score of 0 means that the liquid has not been successfully poured into the cup. score of 100 requires the cup to contain the required liquid and the bottle to be upright. Write PhysEvo. The goal is to write PhysEvo on the table. The score is 0 when no letter is correct, and 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, or 90 when any one, two, three, four, five, or six letters are correct, respectively. All seven letters correct earns 100. The five scores are 100, 100, 100, 75, and 90, with mean Score of 93/100 and an SR of 60%.

sections.title: C ADDITIONAL FRAMEWORK ANALYSIS
sections.content: C.1 CONTROL-INTERFACE COMPARISON focused comparison on language-based object classification evaluates TCP, Joint, and Both interfaces on two scene layouts, for six episodes in total. The model, task skill, initialization for each layout, and budget are held fixed. Mean scores are 40 for TCP, 100 for Joint, and 55 for Both. Joint is retained as the default control interface. The control sequences in figure 3 illustrate two independent executions. The first develops an obstructive posture under TCP/local IK. In the second, Astra adjusts joints after TCP rejection and then completes motion to the same target pose. The mechanism is direct access to the arm configuration, which an end-effector target alone leaves to the IK solver. C.2 OBSERVATION TOOLS Historical-frame retrieval returns images and aligned robot states from earlier in the same episode. It does not advance the environment. Active viewing can place the free wrist camera to the side of manipulation. Geometric tools combine model-selected image features with camera calibration and robot geometry. synthetic-marker reconstruction test accepted 8 of 12 points, with median error of 0.615 mm and 95th-percentile error of 1.437 mm. Four points were rejected by the validity checks. separate wrist-camera translation of approximately 57.525 mm yielded marker error of about 2.14 mm. These component tests measure the calibration and reconstruction paths. Temporal triangulation additionally requires correspondence to the same stationary point across views. C.3 SKILL-GUIDED OBSERVATION AND DIAGNOSIS The pouring example changes the skill guidance while keeping the other loaded skills fixed. The revised skill maintains free-arm side view during pouring, draining, and upright recovery. The task agent uses the observation arm while the pouring arm makes corrections, and the revised episode reaches task success. The packing example reuses trajectory-review tool that presents RGB, robot states, and policy decisions. The meta-agent inspects the box displacement and revises the packing skill to require clearance above the flaps before turn. With the revised skill, the task agent avoids pushing the box away. The reused diagnostic tool thus supports subsequent skill revision.

sections.title: INPUT CONTEXT
sections.content: The system message supplies the control contract and selected skills. Each skill is Markdown text with name and description fields. request also includes the preceding completed tool cycle, current public context, and RGB observations. Key context fields are: { "instruction": "<current task instruction>", "step": <native-step index>, "state": { "left_arm_joint_state": [<six measured joint angles>], "right_arm_joint_state": [<six measured joint angles>], "left_ee_pose": [<x>, <y>, <z>, <qw>, <qx>, <qy>, <qz>], "right_ee_pose": [<x>, <y>, <z>, <qw>, <qx>, <qy>, <qz>], "left_ee_joint_state": [<gripper command echo>], "right_ee_joint_state": [<gripper command echo>], "left_gripper_measured_joints": [<measured finger positions>], "right_gripper_measured_joints": [<measured finger positions>] }, "memory": "<same-episode facts and unresolved questions>", "previous_result": <preceding tool feedback or null>, "budget": { "remaining_native_steps": <integer>, "model_calls_remaining": <integer>, ... }, ... } Named RGB inputs include cam_head, cam_left_wrist, and cam_right_wrist, together with selected previous-segment or requested historical views. Other context fields provide home poses, joint semantics, and camera geometry. Joint angles are in radians; positions are in metres. Task and progress fields. instruction is the natural-language goal for the current task. step is the current native environment-step index: one motion call may advance several native steps, whereas geometry or review call need not advance it. state groups the robots reported measurements at that step. Arm-state fields. left_arm_joint_state and right_arm_joint_state contain six measured joint angles for the corresponding arm. left_ee_pose and right_ee_pose give the reported end-effector position and orientation. In each seven-element pose, the first three entries are x, y, in metres; the final four are the quaternion components in scalar-first order qw, qx, qy, qz. Gripper-state fields. left_ee_joint_state and right_ee_joint_state echo gripper commands. left_gripper_measured_joints and right_gripper_measured_joints instead report measured finger positions. The distinction lets the agent compare what was commanded with what the gripper physically reached; neither closing command nor small opening by itself proves that an object is held. 27 Memory, feedback, and budgets. memory carries the task agents explicit same-episode notes, including established facts and unresolved questions. It is not persistent skill document. previous_result carries the preceding tools feedback, or null when no preceding result is available. budget.remaining_native_steps is the remaining environment-step allowance, while budget.model_calls_remaining is the remaining model-call allowance. These are separate resources because tool call can execute zero, one, or several native steps. Skills and image names. skills name identifies the document and its description summarizes its purpose or applicability; its Markdown body supplies procedural guidance. The named cam_head, cam_left_wrist, and cam_right_wrist inputs identify the source camera for RGB observations. RGB observations are supplied as named image inputs alongside the JSON context. F.2 MODEL OUTPUT AND FUNCTION CALLS The model returns exactly one enabled function call. Every tool requires assessment, plan, phase, and updated episode memory, followed by tool-specific arguments. Below, arguments is displayed as decoded object; the function-call transport serializes it as JSON string. { "type": "function_call", "call_id": "<call identifier>", "name": "control_arms", "arguments": { "assessment": "<observed evidence and uncertainty>", "plan": "<next operation>", "phase": "fine", "memory": "<updated same-episode memory>", "left": null, "right": { "control": "joint", "joints": [<q1>, <q2>, <q3>, <q4>, <q5>, <q6>], "gripper": null }, "steps": <integer>, "settle": <integer> } } Call-envelope fields. type: request and must match the identifier in its return message. name selects an enabled tool, here control_arms; arguments contains the fields validated against that tools schema. function_call marks an executable tool request. call_id identifies that Common decision fields. assessment summarizes the currently observed evidence and remaining uncertainty. plan states the next intended operation. phase selects the fine-motion or transit regime and its permitted segment length. The output memory is the updated note carried into the next decision. 28 Arm-selection fields. left and right select commands for the corresponding arms. non-null arm object uses control: joint to select joint control, joints for its target vector, and gripper for its opening command. An arm or an individual target field set to null preserves that command. steps requests the native motion-segment length, while settle requests additional hold steps for settling. Units and allowed ranges are detailed below. F.3 TOOL ARGUMENTS AND EXECUTION FEEDBACK Table 7 lists tool-specific arguments in addition to the four common fields above. Only enabled tools can be invoked; task-agent calls do not provide shell access or hidden simulator-state queries. Table 7: Task-agent tool arguments. Braced entries denote object fields, and square brackets denote lists.

sections.content: control_arms review_frames project_pixels triangulate_point triangulate_temporal_point verify_completion stop_episode Tool-specific arguments and semantics [{pixel: [{camera, pixel}]. Matches one physical [u,v], z}]. Projects 132 head-view pixels onto [{step, camera}]. Retrieves 16 same-episode RGB frames left, right, steps, settle. Each non-null arm has control, joints, and gripper fields, as shown above. frames: and their public poses without motion. points: model-specified height planes without motion. step, feature, views: feature in 23 distinct current views; returns geometry estimates and diagnostics without motion. step, camera, feature, stationary_target, camera_hand_empty, stationarity_evidence, and samples: [{step, pixel}]. Uses 23 reviewed views from one wrist camera. Both Boolean fields must be true; sampling steps increase, end at the current step, and span at most 24 native steps. No additional arguments. Advances six hold steps and checks native termination. reason. Stops the controller when blocked. Observation and geometry fields. In review_frames, frames is list of retrieval requests: step selects same-episode observation by its native-step index and camera selects its view. In geometric queries, pixel: [u,v] denotes horizontal and vertical image coordinates. The in project_pixels specifies model-chosen height plane in metres; it is hypothesis, not supplied object depth. In triangulate_point, step identifies the current observation, feature describes the same physical feature to match, and views pairs each camera with its pixel coordinates. Temporal geometry and stopping fields. For triangulate_temporal_point, camera selects one wrist camera, feature identifies the target feature, and samples pairs observation steps with its pixel locations. stationary_target and camera_hand_empty state the required stationary-target and empty-camera-hand conditions; stationarity_evidence explains their observational basis. These flags must be supported by the observations. The reason argument of stop_episode explains why execution should stop. 29 Control parameters. Each non-null joints field contains six absolute targets in radians, not joint increments. gripper is continuous opening command in [0, 1]. null arm, joint vector, or gripper field holds its corresponding command. phase is fine or transit: motion segments use 16 or 120 native steps, respectively, with settle in {0, 1, 2}. Execution checks can stop segment before the requested number of steps. Tool-result format. The result is linked to the model call through the same call_id. For motion tool, feedback includes segment status, the executed step count, and tracking measurements. The following abbreviated block displays the serialized output payload as decoded object: { "type": "function_call_output", "call_id": "<same call identifier>", "output": { "feedback": { "status": "<segment status>", "reason": "<status detail>", "executed_steps": <integer>, "tracking": [<per-arm tracking measurements>], ... }, "step": <current native-step index>, "ended": <Boolean> } } The next request supplies updated context and images together with this feedback. Observation and geometry tools instead return their requested evidence or diagnostic information without executing native actions. Return-envelope fields. type: function_call_output identifies tool return. Its call_id links it to the preceding request, and output contains the tools returned payload. As with arguments, the block displays the decoded content rather than the transports JSON string. Execution-feedback fields. feedback.status describes the motion segments execution status, such as completion, interruption, or rejection. feedback.reason provides an associated explanation and may be null when no detail applies. feedback.executed_steps reports how many native steps actually ran, which can differ from the requested motion and settling steps. feedback.tracking contains per-arm measurements comparing commanded and observed execution. Updated step and termination. The returns step is the updated native-step index after the tool call. ended indicates whether the episode has terminated, while task success is determined separately by the environments native evaluator. Updated state, images, and feedback allow the next call to respond to what actually happened.
